questions.stem: A patient who has been on chlorpromazine for 10 years develops involuntary, repetitive tongue protrusions, lip-smacking movements, and facial grimacing that persist even when the medication is held. Which condition does this describe?

options.text: Acute dystonia
Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
Pseudoparkinsonism

questions.rationale: Tardive dyskinesia (TD) develops after months to years of antipsychotic use. It is characterized by involuntary, repetitive, purposeless movements of the face, tongue, and extremities (lip smacking, tongue protrusion, choreiform movements). Key feature: movements PERSIST or worsen when the antipsychotic is reduced/stopped initially. It may be irreversible. VMAT2 inhibitors (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine) are FDA-approved treatments. Acute dystonia (A) is sudden onset within days and responds to anticholinergics. Akathisia (C) is restlessness and urge to move. Pseudoparkinsonism (D) mimics Parkinson's disease.

questions.stem: A patient on lithium for bipolar disorder presents with tremor, ataxia, slurred speech, and confusion. Serum lithium level is 2.4 mEq/L. Which intervention is the priority?

options.text: Hold the next lithium dose and recheck level in 12 hours
Administer activated charcoal to reduce absorption
Discontinue lithium, provide IV normal saline hydration, and prepare for dialysis evaluation
Administer sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine and enhance lithium excretion

questions.rationale: Lithium toxicity: therapeutic range 0.6–1.2 mEq/L. Level 1.5–2.0 = mild toxicity (nausea, tremor, polyuria). Level 2.0–2.5 = moderate toxicity (ataxia, confusion, slurred speech — this patient). Level >2.5 = severe (seizures, coma, cardiac arrest). Moderate-severe toxicity requires: stop lithium, IV NS hydration (promotes renal lithium excretion), and consideration for hemodialysis (most effective removal method). Simply holding a dose (A) is inadequate. Activated charcoal (B) does not bind lithium effectively. Sodium bicarbonate (D) is used for salicylate toxicity, not lithium.

questions.stem: A patient in a long leg cast following tibial fracture reports severe, unrelenting pain rated 9/10 that is not relieved by opioids, along with paresthesia in the foot and tenseness of the cast. Which action is the NURSE'S PRIORITY?

options.text: Administer the PRN opioid analgesic and elevate the extremity above heart level
Assess the 6 P's and notify the provider immediately
Apply ice pack to reduce swelling and reassess in 30 minutes
Loosen the cast padding and document as a comfort measure

questions.rationale: This presentation suggests acute compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion to the injury, unrelieved by analgesia, and paresthesia (early sign of nerve ischemia). The 6 P's (Pain, Pressure, Paralysis, Paresthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness) guide assessment. The nurse must notify the provider IMMEDIATELY — compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency requiring fasciotomy within 6 hours to prevent permanent nerve and muscle damage. Elevating above heart level (A) decreases arterial perfusion, worsening ischemia. Ice (C) and cast loosening (D) delay definitive treatment.

questions.subcategory: Safety and Infection Control / Fall Prevention
questions.stem: A nurse is admitting a 79-year-old patient with a history of orthostatic hypotension, recent fall, and current use of furosemide and lisinopril. Which intervention is HIGHEST priority for fall prevention?

options.text: Place a fall-risk bracelet on the patient and document in the chart
Educate the patient to call for help before getting out of bed and place the call light within reach
Request a physical therapy consult for gait evaluation
Move the patient to a room closer to the nursing station

questions.rationale: The highest-impact, immediately actionable fall prevention measure is patient education combined with environmental setup: instructing the patient to call for assistance before ambulating and ensuring the call light is accessible. This directly addresses the behavioral mechanism of most falls (attempting to get up unassisted) and is executable immediately at the bedside. Applying a fall-risk bracelet without the behavioral intervention does not prevent falls. PT consult and room relocation are appropriate secondary measures but do not provide immediate direct protection.

distractorRationales.a: The safer response addresses infection progression; "Place a fall-risk bracelet on the patient and document in the chart" moves care toward routine care before infection or sepsis escalation.
distractorRationales.c: The option can leave infection progression untreated because it relies on notification without the bedside safety step. "Educate the patient to call for help before getting out of bed and place the call" fits the safer response to the cue "PT consult and room relocation are appropriate secondary measures but do not provide immediate direct protection".
distractorRationales.d: "Move the patient to a room closer to the nursing station" answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. The cue "Applying a fall-risk bracelet without the behavioral intervention does not prevent falls" raises concern for infection progression, so infection or sepsis escalation is needed before routine care.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant is admitted with RSV bronchiolitis. SpO2 is 91% on room air, RR 58, mild intercostal retractions, poor feeding. The physician orders albuterol. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Administer albuterol as ordered; it is the standard of care for RSV bronchiolitis
Question the order; bronchodilators are not recommended as routine treatment for bronchiolitis — prioritize nasal suctioning and supportive care
Hold the albuterol and administer corticosteroids instead
Administer albuterol only if SpO2 drops below 88%

questions.rationale: RSV bronchiolitis is managed with supportive care only per AAP guidelines: nasal suctioning (most effective intervention for symptom relief), adequate hydration (NG feeds if needed), and supplemental O2 for SpO2 <90–92%. Bronchodilators (albuterol) and corticosteroids are NOT recommended because bronchiolitis involves viral-induced inflammation and mucus plugging — not bronchospasm — making bronchodilators ineffective. Multiple RCTs have shown no benefit. The nurse should question the order and clarify before administration. Contact precautions (RSV is spread via droplet/contact) are required.

distractorRationales.a: This distractor shifts care toward misprioritization instead of airway and breathing intervention. The stem cue "supplemental O2 for SpO2 <90–92%" makes oxygenation or ventilation the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.c: The cue "SpO2 is 91% on room air, RR 58, mild intercostal retractions, poor feeding" suggests oxygenation or ventilation, so "Hold the albuterol and administer corticosteroids instead" would not correct the active problem. Airway assessment, positioning, oxygen support, or rapid escalation protects ventilation before teaching or documentation.
distractorRationales.d: The safer response addresses oxygenation or ventilation; "Administer albuterol only if SpO2 drops below 88%" moves care toward routine care before airway and breathing intervention.

questions.takeaway: RSV bronchiolitis = supportive care: nasal suction > bronchodilators; albuterol NOT routine treatment (no bronchospasm mechanism); contact precautions; O2 if SpO2 <90–92%.

questions.subcategory: Safety and Infection Control / Stable vs. Unstable
questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient 4 hours post-cardiac catheterization via right femoral access. The nurse finds the patient diaphoretic, the right groin dressing saturated with blood, and the patient's blood pressure has dropped from 128/76 to 88/50 mmHg. What is the PRIORITY nursing action?

options.text: Apply direct, firm manual pressure to the right groin site immediately
Elevate the foot of the bed and call the provider
Obtain a STAT hemoglobin and hematocrit
Increase the IV fluid rate per standing orders and reassess in 15 minutes

questions.rationale: The patient is showing signs of femoral artery hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability (hypotension, diaphoresis, saturated dressing). The priority is hemorrhage control: applying immediate, firm manual pressure directly over the puncture site. This is the most time-critical intervention to stop ongoing blood loss. Calling the provider and obtaining labs are necessary but are performed concurrently by a second nurse after pressure is established. Trendelenburg positioning is not recommended for vascular hemorrhage, and delaying for 15 minutes risks cardiovascular collapse.

distractorRationales.b: This distractor shifts care toward incomplete escalation instead of bleeding-risk intervention. The stem cue "A nurse is caring for a patient 4 hours post-cardiac catheterization via right femoral access" makes bleeding or anticoagulation injury the active safety concern.
distractorRationales.c: "Obtain a STAT hemoglobin and hematocrit" misses the bedside risk. The cue "After femoral cardiac catheterization, a saturated groin dressing + hypotension = vascular bleeding emergency" points to bleeding or anticoagulation injury. Bleeding risk requires assessment and source control before comfort measures, teaching, or routine medication timing.
distractorRationales.d: The cue "After femoral cardiac catheterization, a saturated groin dressing + hypotension = vascular bleeding emergency" suggests bleeding or anticoagulation injury, so "Increase the IV fluid rate per standing orders and reassess in 15 minutes" would not correct the active problem. Bleeding risk requires assessment and source control before comfort measures, teaching, or routine medication timing.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient at 31 weeks presents with epigastric/RUQ pain, headache, nausea, and malaise. Labs reveal: AST 280 U/L, LDH 950 U/L, platelets 74,000/mm3, hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL with schistocytes on smear, and normal creatinine. Which condition do these findings indicate?

options.text: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP)

questions.stem: A nurse is working at a migrant farmworker health clinic. A patient presents with signs of pesticide exposure: miosis, excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, emesis, and muscle fasciculations. Which class of pesticide is most likely involved and what is the priority antidote?

options.text: Pyrethroid insecticide; administer diphenhydramine for allergic response
Organophosphate or carbamate; administer atropine IV to block muscarinic effects, followed by pralidoxime (2-PAM) for organophosphates
Organochlorine; administer activated charcoal and benzodiazepines
Herbicide (glyphosate); administer IV sodium bicarbonate

questions.rationale: Organophosphate and carbamate pesticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. Muscarinic (DUMBELS): Diarrhea/Defecation, Urination, Miosis, Bradycardia/Bronchospasm/Bronchorrhea, Emesis, Lacrimation, Salivation/Sweating. Nicotinic: muscle fasciculations, weakness, paralysis. CNS: seizures, coma. Antidote: (1) Atropine IV (competitive muscarinic antagonist) — dose titrated to dry secretions, not pupil size; (2) Pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates cholinesterase if given early (before 'aging') — effective for organophosphates, not carbamates. Migrant farmworkers are at high risk due to occupational pesticide exposure.

distractorRationales.a: "Pyrethroid insecticide; administer diphenhydramine for allergic response" misses the bedside risk. The cue "high risk in farmworkers" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.

questions.stem: A nurse is titrating norepinephrine for a patient in septic shock. Current MAP is 58 mmHg on norepinephrine 0.18 mcg/kg/min. Lactate is 5.4 mmol/L. The provider orders vasopressin 0.03 units/min added as a second vasopressor. The nurse understands the rationale for vasopressin addition is PRIMARILY to:

options.text: Replace endogenous vasopressin that is depleted in prolonged septic shock
Improve cardiac output by increasing stroke volume
Reduce the oxygen demand of the myocardium by lowering heart rate
Decrease SVR to improve tissue perfusion in high-output septic shock

questions.rationale: In septic shock, endogenous arginine vasopressin (ADH) stores are depleted within hours due to continuous release during the shock state. Exogenous vasopressin (0.03–0.04 units/min) is added as a fixed-dose adjunct — not titrated — to replace depleted stores and allow reduction ('sparing') of norepinephrine dose (to reduce NE-related adverse effects). Vasopressin acts on V1 receptors to cause vasoconstriction, NOT to improve cardiac output (B) or reduce heart rate (C). It does NOT reduce SVR (D).

distractorRationales.b: The safer response addresses medication toxicity; "Improve cardiac output by increasing stroke volume" moves care toward routine care before medication-safety intervention.
distractorRationales.c: "Reduce the oxygen demand of the myocardium by lowering heart rate" misses the bedside risk. The cue "Vasopressin in septic shock: replaces depleted endogenous stores, allows NE dose reduction (NE-sparing effect)" points to medication toxicity. Medication safety depends on checking contraindications, labs, and adverse effects before giving or continuing the drug.
distractorRationales.d: "Decrease SVR to improve tissue perfusion in high-output septic shock" answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. The cue "Vasopressin in septic shock: replaces depleted endogenous stores, allows NE dose reduction (NE-sparing effect)" raises concern for medication toxicity, so medication-safety intervention is needed before routine care.

questions.takeaway: Vasopressin in septic shock: replaces depleted endogenous stores, allows NE dose reduction (NE-sparing effect). Fixed dose, not titrated.

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism develops sudden-onset temperature 39.8°C, HR 148 with atrial fibrillation, tremor, and confusion after an emergency appendectomy. Which sequence of pharmacologic interventions is CORRECT for thyroid storm?

options.text: Iodine → propylthiouracil (PTU) → propranolol
Propylthiouracil (PTU) → propranolol → iodine (one hour after PTU)
Propranolol → iodine → PTU
Methimazole → iodine → esmolol

questions.rationale: The correct sequence for thyroid storm is: (1) PTU first — blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis AND peripheral T4→T3 conversion; (2) propranolol — controls tachycardia and sympathetic symptoms; (3) iodine (Lugol's solution or SSKI) given at least 1 hour AFTER PTU. Iodine must be given after PTU because iodine provides substrate for thyroid hormone production — if given before a thionamide, it can worsen the storm (Jod-Basedow effect). Methimazole (D) does not block peripheral conversion.

distractorRationales.a: "Iodine → propylthiouracil (PTU) → propranolol" answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. The cue "(2) propranolol — controls tachycardia and sympathetic symptoms" raises concern for medication toxicity, so medication-safety intervention is needed before routine care.
distractorRationales.c: The option can leave medication toxicity untreated because it answers a lower-acuity part of the scenario. "Propylthiouracil (PTU) → propranolol → iodine (one hour after PTU)" fits the safer response to the cue "Never give iodine first".
distractorRationales.d: This distractor shifts care toward misprioritization instead of medication-safety intervention. The stem cue "Never give iodine first" makes medication toxicity the active safety concern.

questions.takeaway: Thyroid storm drug sequence: PTU → propranolol → iodine (1 hour after PTU). Never give iodine first.
